findings.paper_title: Annual Internal Audit Report 24-25 - Audit Committee
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation spending not fully tracked; council cannot currently measure cross-service homelessness costs
findings.detail: The audit found work remains ongoing to 'establish a corporate assessment of spend on homelessness and the provision of accommodation across the organisation' via a shared performance indicator. Currently, spending is tracked separately across services without a consolidated view of total temporary accommodation costs.
findings.matters: Inability to measure total temporary accommodation spending is a gap in financial visibility; if costs are rising (as suggested by the follow-up status), the council has limited ability to monitor or control them.
findings.figures: Total spending not quantified
findings.quote: ongoing examination of options to establish a corporate assessment of spend on homelessness and the provision of accommodation across the organisation in a shared performance reporting indicator on SPAR.

findings.paper_title: Annual Internal Audit Report 24-25 - Audit Committee
findings.headline: HBOP debt recovery suspended for extended period due to staff absence with no recovery monitoring in place
findings.detail: The audit found 'HBOP recovery remains a particular concern, as the one officer working in this area had been absent for a considerable length of time, resulting in a lack of recovery action.' More broadly, 'progress is then not routinely monitored,' meaning bad debts and payment arrangements are not tracked.
findings.matters: A significant debt category (HBOP - Housing Benefit Overpayments) has been effectively inactive due to staffing gaps; lack of routine monitoring creates risk that bad debts accumulate without discovery.
findings.figures: Not quantified
findings.quote: HBOP recovery remains a particular concern, as the one officer working in this area had been absent for a considerable length of time, resulting in a lack of recovery action.

findings.paper_title: Annual Internal Audit Report 24-25 - Audit Committee
findings.headline: SEND deficit requires elimination by end of 2027 under Safety Valve agreement; sector-wide deficit projected to reach £8bn by 2026-27
findings.detail: Torbay is subject to a Safety Valve agreement requiring it to achieve a 'positive in year balance' on the Dedicated Schools Grant deficit 'by the end of 2027.' The audit notes that 'the nationwide SEND deficit currently exceeds £3 billion, projected to rise to £8 billion in 2026-27, presenting significant risks to Council's,' indicating systemic underfunding.
findings.matters: This is a mandatory commitment with a fixed deadline; failure to meet the Safety Valve target exposes the council to financial recovery measures; the sector-wide deficit context shows this is a structural funding problem, not a local issue.
findings.figures: National SEND deficit: £3bn rising to £8bn by 2026-27; Torbay deadline: 31 March 2028
findings.quote: The Council is responsible for implementing a Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) management plan to control and reduce its cumulative deficit, ensuring a positive in year balance by the end of 2027... A recent CIPFA and ALATS article stated that the nationwide SEND deficit currently exceeds £3 billion, projected to rise to £8 billion in 2026-27, presenting significant risks to Council's.

findings.paper_title: Annual Internal Audit Report 24-25 - Audit Committee
findings.headline: Home-to-school transport spending increased 104% since 2018-19 with minimal increase in actual service use
findings.detail: The audit reports 'The H2S cost has increased expeditiously since 2018-19, with the Council seeing an increase of 104% in spend with a minimal increase in service use.' A project has been established to address this, but the cost explosion remains unexplained.
findings.matters: A 104% cost increase in an essential service with no corresponding growth in take-up indicates either inefficiency, cost inflation, or service scope creep; this represents a major unfunded budget pressure on the council.
findings.figures: 104% increase in H2S spend since 2018-19; minimal increase in service use
findings.quote: The H2S cost has increased expeditiously since 2018-19, with the Council seeing an increase of 104% in spend with a minimal increase in service use.

findings.paper_title: ASC Risk Assurance Report
findings.headline: Adult Social Care services received a Limited audit opinion from ASW Assurance in 2024/25.
findings.detail: The Head of Internal Audit at ASW Assurance provided an overall 'Limited' opinion for audit work conducted during 2024/25, based on audits of Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards and Advocacy. This represents a significant control concern in a material service area.
findings.matters: Adult Social Care represents approximately 30% of the council's net budget, so a Limited audit opinion indicates significant governance or control weaknesses in a third of the council's finances, which directly affects lending decisions and council financial resilience.
findings.figures: approximately 30% of the Council's overall net budget for 2025/26
findings.quote: The Head of Internal Audit's opinion, as presented to TSDFT at its Audit and Risk Committee held in June 2025, provided an overall 'Limited' opinion.

findings.paper_title: Turnkey acquisitions for social housing
findings.headline: Business case assumes social rental income will fully service long-term debt financing costs, creating revenue risk if assumptions do not hold
findings.detail: Paper states income generated from social rents of the properties to new tenants will cover the cost of long-term financing of capital debt. Homes will be let to households currently in temporary accommodation or care experienced young people. Business case viability depends on these rental income assumptions and occupancy levels; if rental income is insufficient or void rates exceed assumptions, council revenue budget would need to cover shortfall.
findings.matters: Lenders and finance director need to understand the income model underpinning debt service; actual rental income performance directly affects whether debt is self-financing or requires revenue subsidy
findings.figures: 18 homes; rental income from social rents to households currently in temporary accommodation or care experienced young people
findings.quote: The income generated from the social rents of the properties to the new tenants will cover the cost of long-term financing of the capital debt.

findings.paper_title: Turnkey acquisitions for social housing
findings.headline: Once contracts are exchanged, council cannot withdraw from purchase without penalty, creating commercial commitment risk
findings.detail: Paper notes that property transactions carry commercial risk. Once exchange of contracts occurs, council will not be able to withdraw from purchase without penalty. External conveyancers appointed and independent surveyors will inspect properties and undertake snagging assessments before acquisition proceeds to mitigate identified risks.
findings.matters: Lenders and finance director need to understand the commitment level and that once contracts are exchanged, there are contractual penalties for withdrawal; creates downside risk if due diligence discovers material issues
findings.quote: Once we have exchanged contracts, the Council will not be able to withdraw from the purchase without penalty.

findings.paper_title: Turnkey acquisitions for social housing
findings.headline: Scheme viability entirely contingent on Homes England grant approval, with decision pending until end of summer 2025
findings.detail: Council has bid for Homes England grant to subsidise acquisition and enable tenure conversion to social rent. Officers anticipate the bid will be supported, but paper explicitly states that acquisitions will not proceed if grant is not secured at appropriate level, as scheme would not be viable to deliver social rented housing without subsidy. Grant decision is expected end of summer 2025.
findings.matters: Creates material contingency on capital programme; if Homes England grant is delayed, reduced, or refused, the acquisitions do not proceed and planned housing delivery and revenue cost mitigation are affected
findings.figures: 18 homes (14 + 4); grant decision expected end of summer 2025
findings.quote: In the unlikely event that the Council is unable to secure an appropriate level of Homes England funding the acquisitions will not proceed as it would not be viable to deliver social rented housing without subsidy

findings.paper_title: Turnkey acquisitions for social housing
findings.headline: Council acquiring 18 homes using prudential borrowing from £20m headroom approved by Full Council in May 2025
findings.detail: Cabinet delegating authority to Director of Finance to acquire homes funded through combination of expected Homes England grant (bid submitted, decision pending end of summer 2025), internal affordable housing capital funding, and prudential borrowing. The borrowing will be drawn from the £20m prudential borrowing headroom that was already approved by Cabinet and Council in May 2025.
findings.matters: Material capital commitment that increases council debt position; lenders and finance director need to understand the scale, financing structure, and headroom utilization
findings.figures: £20m prudential borrowing headroom (approved May 2025); 18 homes total acquisition (14 + 4); exact borrowing amount not specified in main paper
findings.quote: To fund the required long-term borrowing from the £20m prudential borrowing headroom agreed by Full Council in May 2025

findings.paper_title: Budget Monitoring – Revenue and Capital Outturn 2025 26 Quarter 1 Revised Officer Report
findings.headline: Council approving £2.5m additional borrowing to lend to wholly-owned waste company SWISCo
findings.detail: Council is proposing to borrow £2.5m to make capital loans to SWISCo for phased fleet modernization over 30 months. SWISCo will repay the loans including interest over 7 years from operational revenue budget.
findings.matters: Council taking on new borrowing to lend to own company; loan repayment is contingent on SWISCo's operational performance and financial viability
findings.figures: £2.5m borrowing; 7-year repayment by SWISCo from revenue budget
findings.quote: That Council approve the additional borrowing of £2.5m to facilitate capital loans to SWISCO to enable them to modernise their fleet

findings.paper_title: Budget Monitoring – Revenue and Capital Outturn 2025 26 Quarter 1 Revised Officer Report
findings.headline: Capital program expanded to £52.2m including £5.4m new borrowing for Levelling Up Fund match
findings.detail: Council has increased its approved capital budget from £32.6m to £52.2m at Q1. The expansion includes £5.4m of new borrowing required to match-fund £20m in Levelling Up Fund grants for Brixham Port and Paignton Tech Park regeneration projects.
findings.matters: Significant expansion of capital program and new borrowing increases council leverage; ability to deliver large program on time and budget will impact financial position
findings.figures: Capital program revised to £52.239m from £32.606m approved; £5.4m required borrowing for grant match
findings.quote: with the Council required to match fund a total of £5.4m through supported borrowing, subject to an approved business case.

findings.paper_title: Budget Monitoring – Revenue and Capital Outturn 2025 26 Quarter 1 Revised Officer Report
findings.headline: Overall revenue budget projecting £785k overspend by year end despite mitigation efforts
findings.detail: The council is forecasting a £785k (0.5%) revenue overspend for 2025/26. While modest in percentage terms, this reflects continued cost pressures across services that require active mitigation to achieve breakeven.
findings.matters: Q1 overspend projections, even if modest, indicate sustained budget pressure; full-year outcome depends on successful delivery of mitigating actions
findings.figures: £785k projected overspend on total budget of £148.288m
findings.quote: The Council is currently projecting an overspend of £785k by the end of the year.

findings.paper_title: Budget Monitoring – Revenue and Capital Outturn 2025 26 Quarter 1 Revised Officer Report
findings.headline: DSG Higher Needs Block deficit of £14.5m remains major liability despite DfE Safety Valve support
findings.detail: The council has accumulated a £14.469m Dedicated Schools Grant deficit from prior years. The DfE has funded £8.777m under the Safety Valve program and committed to writing off the remainder if recovery targets are hit, but council remains heavily dependent on continued DfE support and successful plan delivery.
findings.matters: £14.5m contingent liability dependent on external government support and recovery plan execution represents significant downside risk if targets are missed or funding withdrawn
findings.figures: £14.469m cumulative DSG deficit, £8.777m funded by DfE to date, £943k forecast overspend in 2025/26
findings.quote: without which the DSG cumulative deficit would have been £14.469 at the end of 25/26. It is critical that the Council continues to deliver on its recovery plan

findings.paper_title: Budget Monitoring – Revenue and Capital Outturn 2025 26 Quarter 1 Revised Officer Report
findings.headline: Legal Services £543k overspend despite multiple budget increases in recent years
findings.detail: Legal Services has received several budget increases to address demand and recruitment challenges, but is still overspending. The persistent overspend is driven by difficulty recruiting permanent staff, requiring expensive agency cover.
findings.matters: Repeated budget increases have not resolved the underlying cost structure problem, suggesting the overspend may be structural and difficult to eliminate
findings.figures: £543k overspend on budget of £2.085m, projected outturn £2.628m
findings.quote: The service continues to experience financial challenges despite significant budget increases in recent years to reflect increasing demand for the service and difficulties in recruiting permanent staff.

findings.paper_title: Budget Monitoring – Revenue and Capital Outturn 2025 26 Quarter 1 Revised Officer Report
findings.headline: Children's social care placement costs overrunning by £443k due to market shortage
findings.detail: The council is overspending on children's social care placements because shortage of suitable placements in the market is forcing higher-cost residential placements. This is a market-driven cost issue rather than council inefficiency.
findings.matters: Placement cost inflation driven by market shortage is a structural statutory service pressure beyond council control; indicates persistent upward cost trajectory
findings.figures: £443k overspend on budget of £23.559m, projected outturn £24.002m
findings.quote: A shortage of suitable available placements continues to drive up costs within the market and we have recently had to make some high-cost residential placements.

findings.paper_title: Record of Decision Turnkey Acquisitions for Social Housing
findings.headline: Torbay has 1,600 households registered for social housing and 160 in temporary accommodation
findings.detail: The paper states Torbay faces acute housing challenges with substantial existing demand. These acquisitions directly serve current need, targeting households in temporary accommodation and care experienced young people, rather than speculative expansion.
findings.matters: Demonstrates the scale of housing pressure the council is addressing and shows this capital deployment meets genuine unmet demand
findings.figures: 1,600 households registered for social housing, approximately 160 in temporary accommodation at any time
findings.quote: Torbay faced acute housing challenges, with 1,600 households registered for social housing and around 160 in temporary accommodation at any time.

findings.paper_title: Record of Decision Turnkey Acquisitions for Social Housing
findings.headline: Acquisition is conditional on securing Homes England grant that subsidises the purchase price
findings.detail: The decision explicitly requires securing an acceptable Homes England grant allocation before proceeding, with the grant intended to subsidise acquisitions and enable conversion to social rent. If grant funding is not secured, the council will need to revisit the financial model and borrowing requirements.
findings.matters: Actual borrowing requirement and scheme viability depend on external grant funding that is not guaranteed, creating contingency risk for capital deployment
findings.figures: Homes England grant amount to be negotiated
findings.quote: subject to the satisfactory completion of all due diligence and securing an acceptable allocation of grant funding from Homes England

findings.paper_title: Record of Decision Turnkey Acquisitions for Social Housing
findings.headline: Council commits to acquire 18 homes using £20m prudential borrowing headroom
findings.detail: Cabinet approved acquisition of 14 homes at Site A and 4 homes at Site B through turnkey arrangements. Funding comes from the £20m prudential borrowing headroom approved by Full Council in May 2025, supplemented by internal capital funding allocations. This reduces borrowing requirements while delivering a financially viable scheme.
findings.matters: Shows deployment of significant prudential borrowing capacity to a specific capital project, affecting future borrowing flexibility
findings.figures: 14 homes at Site A, 4 homes at Site B, £20m prudential borrowing headroom
findings.quote: the required long-term borrowing be funded from the £20m prudential borrowing headroom agreed by Full Council in May 2025

findings.paper_title: Local Account Summary Adult Social Care 2024-25 Appendix
findings.headline: Finance and billing complaints are the largest complaint category, suggesting cost management concerns
findings.detail: During 2024-25, ASC received 45 complaints and concerns, with finance and billing accounting for 41% of the total (the largest theme). The response included updating charging policy leaflets and increasing staff awareness, suggesting cost communication remains problematic.
findings.matters: High proportion of billing complaints may indicate service users/families are experiencing unexpected or unclear costs, relevant to financial sustainability and reputational risk.
findings.figures: 45 total complaints/concerns; 41% (largest category) related to finance and billing
findings.quote: Key themes identified included finance and billing (41%), communication (22%), and service delivery (16%).

findings.paper_title: Local Account Summary Adult Social Care 2024-25 Appendix
findings.headline: Demographic shift to older population creates structural long-term fiscal pressure
findings.detail: Torbay's population aged 65+ is currently 27% and projected to increase to 34% by 2043. The working-age population (18-64) is expected to fall from 55% to 50%. This demographic composition change is steeper than England-wide trends and directly drives adult social care demand, creating a structural constraint that cannot be managed through efficiency gains alone.
findings.matters: Structural aging creates embedded long-term fiscal pressure on councils; lenders need to understand this is not a cyclical problem but a permanent shift in service demand.
findings.figures: Current over-65s: 27% of population; projected 2043: 34%; working age (18-64) falling from 55% to 50%; total population rising from 139,485 to 153,088 by 2043
findings.quote: 27% of our population is over 65 years of age which is set to increase to 34% during the next 20 years.

findings.paper_title: Local Account Summary Adult Social Care 2024-25 Appendix
findings.headline: Sustained demand growth across multiple adult social care metrics signals structural pressure
findings.detail: New support requests increased 5.5%; mental health needs showed 7.6% rise following similar 6.9% growth in 2023-24; carers registered increased 6.9%; home care demand rose 6.3%; long-term care clients grew 4.5%. The document describes mental health growth as 'a continuing trend' indicating persistent upward pressure.
findings.matters: Persistent demand growth above supply capacity signals unfunded service pressures that will require either cuts, cost containment, or additional funding.
findings.figures: New requests +5.5% (to 2,584); mental health +7.6% (to 916); carers +6.9% (to 5,764); home care +6.3% (to 2,141); long-term care clients +4.5% (to 2,736)
findings.quote: The number of people with identified mental health needs who were supported by services again saw a notable increase in 2024-25 on the previous year (+7.6%). This followed a similar increase in 2023-24 of +6.9%.

findings.paper_title: Local Account Summary Adult Social Care 2024-25 Appendix
findings.headline: Adult social care spending variance being addressed through council reserves
findings.detail: The document states that actual spending on care has exceeded budgets set, and this variance is being addressed through a transformation programme funded by council reserves. The council income contribution to the Integrated Care Organisation was £65.615m, with net expenditure on care totalling £82.3m in 2024-25.
findings.matters: Councils drawing down reserves to manage service spending above budget indicates financial stress and erodes buffers available for future pressures or emergencies.
findings.figures: Council income contribution 2024/25: £65.615m; net expenditure on care: £82.3m; gross expenditure: £105.9m
findings.quote: Partners are working closely together on a joint adult social care transformation programme (using identified council reserves), to identify improvements and efficiencies to the current operating model in Torbay to address the variance in budgets set and costs accrued

findings.paper_title: Record of Decision Acquisition of Land for the Delivery of Affordable Housing
findings.headline: The council is drawing down a £1.2m ringfenced reserve to acquire land for 14 affordable homes
findings.detail: Cabinet allocated £1.2m to a ringfenced housing revenue reserve in May 2025 and has now approved deploying it to acquire a Brixham site for approximately 14 affordable homes. The acquisition is intended to 'reduce reliance on costly temporary accommodation' and requires no additional borrowing.
findings.matters: A lender would want to understand how the council is deploying its reserves and whether temporary accommodation costs represent a material, ongoing budget pressure
findings.figures: £1.2m reserve, approximately 14 affordable homes
findings.quote: The acquisition was to be funded from the £1.2 million ringfenced housing revenue reserve, with no additional borrowing required, unlocking new housing supply, reducing pressure on temporary accommodation

findings.paper_title: Budget Monitoring – Revenue and Capital Outturn 2025 26 Quarter 1
findings.headline: Overall revenue overspend of £785k at Q1; multiple services carrying mitigations via Financial Sustainability Plans
findings.detail: The council is projecting a £785k overspend by year-end (£148.288m actual against £147.503m budget). Multiple services—including Adult Social Care transformation, children's placements, homelessness, heritage asset management, and legal services—are being managed through Financial Sustainability Plans. Robust financial management 'continues to be required' from all services.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the £785k forecast will hold; the document shows overspends are concentrated in services (children, legal, DSG) where underlying cost drivers are structural, not cyclical.
findings.figures: £785k projected overspend on £147.503m budget; Children's Services £558k, Corporate Services £563k overspend; DSG additional £943k not in main table
findings.quote: Robust financial management and control continues to be required from all services across the Council in order to mitigate current and emerging spending pressures to ultimately achieve a breakeven position by the year end.

findings.paper_title: Budget Monitoring – Revenue and Capital Outturn 2025 26 Quarter 1
findings.headline: External audit fees increasing by £200k, attributed to national backlog of local authority audits
findings.detail: The council's external audit fees are expected to exceed budget by £200k in 2025/26. The document attributes this to national increases in costs and the backlog of audits for Local Authority accounts.
findings.matters: Rising audit costs can signal governance risks or audit complexity; the national backlog suggests audit delays and potential weaknesses in financial reporting timelines across the sector.
findings.figures: £200k overspend on external audit fees against a budget of £0.319m
findings.quote: Our External Audit fees for the year are expected to exceed budget by £200k in 2025/26, due to increase in costs and follows on from the national issue relating to the backlog of audits for Local Authority accounts.

findings.paper_title: Budget Monitoring – Revenue and Capital Outturn 2025 26 Quarter 1
findings.headline: Property holding costs overrunning by £600k as income on vacant/regeneration sites falls
findings.detail: The council is estimating a £600k overspend on costs for holding property pending longer-term regeneration, including Union Square where rental income has fallen and the council is absorbing costs previously met by tenants. The council plans to fund this from one-off reserves.
findings.matters: Regeneration schemes carrying rising holding costs signal execution delays or changing market conditions; using one-off reserves to cover structural cost increases is not sustainable.
findings.figures: £600k estimated overspend on property holding costs
findings.quote: We are estimating an overspend of £600k in relation to the additional costs in holding property, pending longer term regeneration. This includes suites such as Union Square where the level of rental income has reduced and additional costs are being incurred that previously would have been met from tenants.

findings.paper_title: Budget Monitoring – Revenue and Capital Outturn 2025 26 Quarter 1
findings.headline: Levelling Up Fund award of £20m carries £5.4m match-funding requirement via supported borrowing
findings.detail: Torbay was awarded £20m in the third round of Levelling Up Funds for Brixham Port and Paignton Technology Park projects. The total scheme cost is £25.415m, requiring the council to match fund £5.4m through supported borrowing, subject to business case approval.
findings.matters: This is conditional borrowing that commits the council to £5.4m of new debt; a lender needs to understand whether the projects will generate sufficient return or savings to justify the borrowing.
findings.figures: £20m grant awarded; £25.415m total scheme cost; £5.4m match funding required via supported borrowing
findings.quote: Torbay was awarded £20m, which has been allocated between these projects. The total cost is estimated at £25.415m, with the Council required to match fund a total of £5.4m through supported borrowing, subject to an approved business case.

findings.paper_title: Budget Monitoring – Revenue and Capital Outturn 2025 26 Quarter 1
findings.headline: Council approving £4m new borrowing for SWISCo fleet modernisation
findings.detail: The council is being asked to approve £4m of additional prudential borrowing to provide a capital loan to its wholly owned company SWISCo. The loan is to replace ageing vehicles to avoid mounting repairs, maintenance, and hire costs. SWISCo will repay the loan from its revenue budget over 10 years.
findings.matters: New borrowing increases the council's debt and relies on SWISCo's ability to service it from operations; a lender needs to see the underlying business case and SWISCo's financial stability.
findings.figures: £4m new prudential borrowing; drawn down over 10 years; repaid from SWISCo revenue budget
findings.quote: A further business case has been prepared and reviewed by Finance, which would provide an additional loan to support a phased replacement of ageing vehicles in order to avoid expensive repairs and hire costs.

findings.paper_title: Budget Monitoring – Revenue and Capital Outturn 2025 26 Quarter 1
findings.headline: Higher Needs DSG deficit: £943k overspend forecast despite Safety Valve agreement; £14.5m historical deficit
findings.detail: Outside the main council budget, the Dedicated Schools Grant higher needs block is forecasting a £943k overspend for 2025/26. The council is part of the DfE Safety Valve programme and has received £8.777m in support, but the cumulative deficit was £14.469m before that payment. Achieving the recovery plan targets 'continues to be challenging'.
findings.matters: DSG deficits sit above the council's normal borrowing and must be recovered across future years; the deficit is persistent and the council is already off-track against its safety valve plan.
findings.figures: £943k overspend forecast 2025/26; £14.469m cumulative DSG deficit (before DfE support); £8.777m already received from DfE
findings.quote: Achieving the targets outlined and agreed within Safety Valve Plan continues to be challenging and an overspend of £943k is now being forecast for 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: Budget Monitoring – Revenue and Capital Outturn 2025 26 Quarter 1
findings.headline: Legal Services overspending by £543k due to persistent recruitment failures and agency staff reliance
findings.detail: Legal services is forecasting a £543k overspend. Despite significant budget increases in recent years, the council continues to struggle to recruit permanent staff and has had to rely on agency staff to cover vacancies and absences. A financial sustainability plan review is being brought forward.
findings.matters: A budget line that overruns despite two years of increases suggests the council has not solved the underlying problem and may face further unfunded pressures in this area.
findings.figures: £543k overspend against a budget of £2.085m; budget has been increased 'in recent years'
findings.quote: The Legal Services budget is projecting an overspend of £543k. The service continues to experience financial challenges despite significant budget increases in recent years to reflect increasing demand for the service and difficulties in recruiting permanent staff.

findings.paper_title: Budget Monitoring – Revenue and Capital Outturn 2025 26 Quarter 1
findings.headline: Children's social care placement costs overrunning by £443k despite placement shortage being a known, recurring issue
findings.detail: The council is forecasting a £443k overspend on children's social care placements. The document states this is driven by a shortage of suitable placements driving up market costs and notes the council has had to make some high-cost residential placements. This pressure is material and ongoing.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether service pressures are controllable or structural; placement market shortages suggest this overspend will recur and may worsen.
findings.figures: £443k overspend on children's social care placements (excl. UASC) against a budget of £23.559m
findings.quote: A shortage of suitable available placements continues to drive up costs within the market and we have recently had to make some high-cost residential placements.
